Recently it was announced that Columbia Pictures is developing a remake of the 1984 John Carpenter film Starman. It's one of my favorite films, and although I'm really, REALLY opposed to a remake, here are 3 ways to do it so that it might not be terrible:

Make It A Quasi Sequel

Instead of a direct remake of the original, perhaps make it a sequel with new characters and a different alien from the same planet. There could be some neat references to the 'incident from 1984' while giving us a new alien with a new perspective.

Set It In A Different Country

Neill Blomkamp's District 9 proved that a good Sci-Fi film doesn't have to take place in America.

Gender Flip The Two Main Roles

One way to differentiate the remake from the original is to gender flip the two main characters, with the new alien becoming a clone of the deceased wife of widower 'John' Hayden. If done right this could offer a fresh new take on the film and make the remake different enough from the original to stand on it's own.

All that being said, I think Hollywood has gone remake crazy, and I was upset when I first heard that Starman was being remade.
3 Ways To The Do The STARMAN Remake

Let's go back a few years. Hollywood has decided they need to remake The Thing [1982]. Cult classic, beloved by many, already two films based off of a short story.

As opposed to a remake, it was a prequel detailing with the Norwegian team. Carpenter did some mastercraft filmmaking in horror building up the unease, and mystery surrounding this team, and their downfall.

How do you recast Kurt Russel in the 80s? Answer is you don't, by making it a prequel, you don't need to have one to one characters, and you can make a new character that's a woman. Can even cast a "scream queen" in the role that is already fairly well known, but not super popular.

Here's what happened. It was a prequel. It also was a beat for beat remake of Carpenter's flick, just without any of the suspense, and filled with cheap CGI that shat on the special fx of the 80s film. It's only good moment? When they transitioned from their film into the 80s film, using the original score, and shot.

It is all about grabbing as many titles from the 80s, and 90s, that haven't been remade yet, that they hope they can trick the older fans to see the new version, while using the innate brand of the film to sell it to the new generation. And honestly, everyone knows The Force Awakens was a remake, made insane money, so they're not going to stop any time soon.
